description: 🚀 We are Orbital Insight , a team of students passionate about coding, space exploration, science, and 3D visualization. We aim to build an intuitive tool for comparing lunar South Pole landing sites. Join us to combine technology and creativity while solving a real space-planning challenge. We’re looking for members skilled in astronomy, physics, React/Three.js, UI/UX, backend development, data visualization, or research.
summary:
Orbital Insight is a lunar South Pole landing-site explorer developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge (CLPS domain). It enables users to compare candidate landing sites by evaluating the factors that most influence mission success: Sun position and illumination, direct-to-Earth visibility and communication windows, and terrain context in 2D/3D.

The application addresses the challenge of South Pole mission planning, where low Sun angles, obstructed horizons, and competing site trade-offs make analysis complex. Orbital Insight integrates real NASA data—including LOLA topography, LOLA long-term illumination and Earth-visibility maps, and NAIF SPICE kernels—to compute site-specific geometry and conditions. Its results are validated against JPL Horizons to better than 0.0001°, and every displayed value is clearly labeled as MEASURED, DERIVED, or SIMULATED to ensure transparency and traceability.

This is important because landing-site selection directly affects power generation, communications, and operational safety. By providing credible, side-by-side comparisons grounded in authoritative data, Orbital Insight supports more informed, trustworthy mission planning decisions.
details:
What the project does and how it works

Orbital Insight is a browser-based lunar South Pole landing-site explorer for NASA Space Apps Challenge (CLPS domain). It helps users compare candidate sites by answering four mission-critical questions: where the Sun is at a chosen time, whether Earth is visible for direct-to-Earth (DTE) communication, how much illumination a site receives over a lunar day, and what the local terrain/horizon looks like.

How it works:

  • Data pipeline (Python): Downloads and processes authoritative NASA products, including LOLA 5 m and 240 m topography DEMs, LOLA long-term average solar illumination and Earth-visibility maps, and NAIF SPICE kernels (DE440s planetary ephemeris, lunar frame/orientation kernels, leapseconds).
  • Scientific computation: Uses SPICE (via spiceypy) to compute Sun/Earth azimuth, elevation, and range in the MOON_ME frame; derives south-polar stereographic coordinates; reads GeoTIFF DEMs; ray-casts terrain horizon profiles; and computes lit fraction, longest sunlit/dark periods, and Earth-visibility windows over a sampled lunar day.
  • Runtime service: A lightweight Python HTTP API (server.py) serves the derived site catalog/provenance and performs date-specific geometry calculations on demand using precomputed horizons and loaded SPICE kernels.
  • Frontend app: A React/Vite web app provides a landing page, mission planner, and site comparison view. Users select a site, UTC time, and observer height (e.g., 1 m lander / 5 m habitat) to see instant geometry, lunar-day timelines, long-term averages, and a 3D Moon/site visualization.

Benefits and intended impact

  • Supports better mission decisions: Makes trade-offs visible (illumination vs. communication vs. terrain obstruction) for South Pole sites where small horizon differences have large operational consequences.
  • Trustworthy, transparent analysis: Every displayed value is labeled MEASURED, DERIVED, or SIMULATED, with provenance/citations shown to users.
  • Reduces tool fragmentation: Brings together ephemeris, terrain horizon, and illumination analysis—typically spread across GIS, SPICE workflows, and spreadsheets—into one interactive comparison interface.
  • Educational impact: Helps judges, planners, students, and the public understand why polar landing is difficult through interpretable numbers, timelines, and 3D context.

Tools, languages, hardware, and software used

  • Languages: JavaScript/JSX, Python, CSS/HTML
  • Frontend: React 19, React Router, Vite, Tailwind CSS v4, Three.js with React Three Fiber and Drei, Lucide React
  • Backend/pipeline: Python, spiceypy, NumPy, tifffile, imagecodecs, pypdf, custom modules for geometry/projection/DEM/horizon/illumination, standard-library threaded HTTP server
  • Data sources/software services: NASA PGDA LOLA datasets (site DEMs, wide DEM, long-term illumination/Earth-visibility maps), NAIF SPICE kernels (including DE440s), Moon Trek/LROC resources for visualization context, JPL Horizons used for validation
  • Development tooling: npm, Vite dev server/build, oxlint; reproducible pipeline scripts and manifests (SHA-256/metadata) for downloaded NASA data
  • Hardware: Developed on standard consumer/developer computers (no specialized hardware required to run the app beyond typical CPU/RAM for local processing and 3D rendering)

How the project is creative

  • Unified “decision view”: Combines terrain-aware horizon modeling, real ephemeris geometry, and long-term NASA illumination products in a single, user-facing workflow tailored to CLPS-style site comparison.
  • Explainable science UX: Treats provenance and uncertainty labeling as first-class interface elements, not afterthoughts—turning scientific rigor into a core user experience feature.
  • Practical engineering creativity: Implements a custom GeoTIFF floating-point predictor/TIFF decoding path (using tifffile and hand-written decoding) to work around environment constraints where GDAL/rasterio binaries were blocked.
  • Multi-audience design: Balances credible metrics for technical users with visual/interactive explanations (timeline, 3D scene) for learners and general audiences.

Factors the team considered

  • Scientific correctness and validation: Used MOON_ME-consistent frames/projections, applied apparent positions (light-time/aberration), and validated Sun/Earth geometry against JPL Horizons (< 0.0001° difference) and cross-checked illumination behavior against published Barker et al. results.
  • Data integrity and traceability: Prioritized verified NASA sources, recorded download manifests/provenance, and enforced strict labeling rules so no value is presented without context.
  • Usability and clarity: Focused on the few questions that drive mission outcomes, exposed assumptions (e.g., observer height, averaging windows, sampling period), and designed for planners, educators, and public users.
  • Constraints and reproducibility: Considered offline/reproducible processing after downloads, resumable verified data retrieval, and implementation choices that work within platform/security limitations while preserving accuracy
